steps.explanationAfterStep: The peroxyacid adds to the ketone carbon. The C=O π electrons move onto oxygen, giving an alkoxide next to a protonated peroxide oxygen.
Also correct: the addition and the proton transfer drawn as one step. The textbook draws them as two.
A proton transfer gives the neutral Criegee intermediate, a peroxy ester on a tetrahedral carbon.

The key step. The weak O–O bond breaks and 3-chlorobenzoate leaves; at the same time the bridgehead carbon moves from the ring carbon to the oxygen, inserting an oxygen into the ring. The bridgehead CH migrates rather than the CH₂ because it is more substituted. It moves with retention of configuration, so the bicyclic shape, and the stereochemistry Corey set in the Diels–Alder step, survive (not checked by the app yet).
The carboxylate takes the proton, giving the neutral lactone and 3-chlorobenzoic acid.

title: Baeyer–Villiger in a bicycle
subtitle: The bridgehead carbon migrates and inserts an oxygen into the bicyclic ketone
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 36 (the Baeyer–Villiger reaction)
E. J. Corey, N. M. Weinshenker, T. K. Schaaf and W. Huber, Stereo-controlled synthesis of dl-prostaglandins F2α and E2, J. Am. Chem. Soc., 1969, 91, 5675–5677

criegee.caption: the Criegee intermediate
hintTiers: The weak O–O bond breaks and a carboxylate leaves. As it goes, a group on the carbon moves to the oxygen it leaves behind. The more substituted group, the one best at carrying positive charge, migrates.
The two groups on the carbon are a ring CH₂ and the bridgehead CH. The bridgehead CH, a secondary carbon, migrates; the OH lone pair forms the C=O.
O–O bond → lone pair on the carboxylate oxygen; the C–C bond to the bridgehead carbon → new bond from the bridgehead carbon to the oxygen still on the ring; OH lone pair → C=O π bond.
criegee.learnerPrompt: A group moves from carbon to oxygen as the O–O bond breaks. Which group, and to which oxygen?

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The CH₂ could migrate in principle, but the more substituted bridgehead carbon migrates: it carries the partial positive charge better. Corey obtained a single lactone.
The migrating carbon moves to the oxygen bonded to the ring carbon, the one left electron-poor as the O–O bond breaks. The other oxygen leaves with the carboxylate.
The O–O bond breaks towards the carboxylate oxygen: the carboxylate is the leaving group, stabilised by resonance.
That would lose the peroxyacid again. Keep it and let the O–O bond break.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: the carboxylate leaves and the bridgehead carbon moves. The ring carbon has lost a bond: the OH lone pair makes up for it.

reactants.caption: the bicyclic ketone + mCPBA
hintTiers: A Baeyer–Villiger oxidation starts like any addition to a ketone: a nucleophile adds to the carbonyl carbon. Here the nucleophile is the peroxyacid.
The terminal O–H oxygen of the peroxyacid adds to the ketone carbon; the C=O π bond moves onto oxygen.
Lone pair of the peroxyacid's OH oxygen → new bond to the ketone carbon; ketone C=O π bond → lone pair on the ketone oxygen.
reactants.learnerPrompt: The peroxyacid adds to the ketone. Draw the addition.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: mCPBA can epoxidise alkenes, but this strained bicyclic ketone reacts faster, and Corey used one equivalent of peroxyacid with NaHCO₃ as a buffer. Attack the ketone.
The peroxide oxygen next to the C=O is part of the leaving group. The nucleophile is the terminal OH oxygen.
Oxygen does not attack oxygen. The ketone carbon is the electrophile: the peroxyacid adds to it.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: the peroxyacid oxygen attacks the ketone carbon. Which bond must move so that carbon keeps four bonds?

zwitterion.caption: the first adduct: alkoxide and oxonium in one molecule
hintTiers: The molecule has an O⁻ and an O⁺–H next to each other. A proton transfer neutralises both.
The alkoxide oxygen takes the proton from the positive oxygen.
Alkoxide lone pair → new bond to the O⁺–H hydrogen; that O–H bond → lone pair on the positive oxygen.
zwitterion.learnerPrompt: Move the proton to make the Criegee intermediate.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Migration comes after the proton transfer: a neutral Criegee intermediate loses a carboxylate, not a carboxylic acid. Move the proton first.
That undoes the addition. Move the proton to the alkoxide instead.

protonated-lactone.caption: the protonated lactone + 3-chlorobenzoate
hintTiers: The lactone carbonyl oxygen carries a proton and a positive charge. A base is close by.
The 3-chlorobenzoate that just left takes the proton.
Carboxylate oxygen lone pair → new bond to the O–H hydrogen; that O–H bond → lone pair on the lactone oxygen.
protonated-lactone.learnerPrompt: Finish: remove the proton from the lactone.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Adding the carboxylate to the lactone carbon is unproductive: it would only fall apart again. Take the proton instead.

mechanismSummary: mCPBA adds to the bicyclic ketone, and a proton transfer gives the Criegee intermediate. The O–O bond breaks and 3-chlorobenzoate leaves as the bridgehead carbon moves from carbon to oxygen. Of the two groups on the ketone carbon, the more substituted (the bridgehead CH, not the CH₂) migrates, so a single lactone forms: 2-oxabicyclo[3.2.1]oct-6-en-3-one with the CH₂OMe group on its one-carbon bridge. The migrating carbon keeps its configuration, so the relative stereochemistry of the ring carbons is unchanged (explained, not yet checked by the app). The C=C survives: with one equivalent of peroxyacid, the strained ketone reacts first. Bridged bicycles are hard to draw flat; the drawing shows the six-membered ring with the one-carbon bridge on top.
